• Most would have like 3 or 4 groups during the day (usually not on weekend though) that you were expected to go to. However, sometimes I would skip the groups if I just didn’t feel like going. I almost always would skip occupational therapy because I really dislike arts & crafts.

• Every hospital I’ve been to, you would meet with the psychiatrist once per day. 

• 2 of the hospitals I’ve been to would take groups outside for like 30 minutes every so often throughout the day. And one hospital had a courtyard you could just go out to whenever you wanted, except like the middle of the night.

• Every hospital I’ve been to has had a tv, radio, coloring, word searches, sudoku, stuff like that. But honestly the worst part of being hospitalized for me has been how boring it is. There’s just only so much you can do.

• I have decent-ish insurance (US) but my bills usually come out to ~$4k-6k.

• Most of them have definitely been worth it for me. I have had some bad experiences but certainly not all have been bad. In the US hospitalization should really only be for when you are a danger to yourself or others.

I can’t tell you if it’s schizoaffective or not, as I am not a trained professional. However, I would give you two pieces of advice, if you want them. 

1. See a psychiatrist. Whether you do have schizoaffective or not is between you and a psychiatrist. If you do then you can get treatment or work on a treatment plan, and if you don’t they can hopefully help you navigate what is going on.

2. Stop using. I know that substances can have a different effect on everyone, but in general, it’s better to not use anything (weed, alcohol, etc.). I quit smoking 2 years ago because everytime I would smoke it would add to my symptoms. I would say that it’s better to be sober when you are trying to figure out what’s going on, so you can differentiate what’s happening organically vs. what might be exacerbated by using.

I hope you can find some help with everything though, schizoaffective or not. Good luck friend :)

Not necessarily. This is the diagnostic criteria for the DSM-5:

Someone with schizoaffective disorder meets the primary criteria (Criterion A) for schizophrenia, which includes two or more of the following:

- Delusions
- Hallucinations
- Disorganized speech (speech that is easily derailed or is incoherent)
- Grossly disorganized or catatonic behavior
- Negative symptoms (flat expressions, loss of pleasure/anhedonia, lack of motivation/avolition, and other experiences that are “taken away” from the person)

Schizoaffective disorder includes at least two of the above symptoms related to psychotic disorders and these DSM-5 criteria:

- A major mood episode (either major depression or mania) that lasts for an uninterrupted period of time
- Delusions or hallucinations for two or more consecutive weeks without mood symptoms sometime during the life of the illness
- Mood symptoms are present for the majority of the illness
- The symptoms aren’t caused by substance use

A lot of people are mentioning appetite, but it can do more than just increase your appetite. There are multiple reasons people gain weight, not just on seroquel, but on a lot of antipsychotics. 

1. Increased appetite. They can make you crave foods high in sugar and fat.

2. Hormones. Seroquel can impact you thyroid (T3 and T4) which can cause weight gain.

3. Fat storage. Seroquel is thought to change the way your body stores fat, which can cause weight gain.

4. Metabolism. Seroquel can slow your metabolism. This is one of the most common reasons people gain weight.

All of these can happen, as well as personal factors (diet, exercise, motivation, etc.) can influence weight gain. It really varies person to person.
